references.text: The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every thought and plan in their hearts was evil all day long.
God looked at the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all people had corrupted their way on the earth.
Then God said to Noah, 'I have decided to put an end to all people, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. Behold, I will destroy them along with the earth.'
Is it a small thing for the house of Judah to do the abominable things they do here? For they have filled the land with violence and provoke my wrath again and again.
Prepare the chain! For the land is full of bloodshed, and the city is full of violence.

By faith Noah, being divinely warned about things not yet seen, in godliness built an ark to save his family. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
Thematic parallel: God's wrath over sin leads to the destruction of the earth.
Prophetic precursor and parallel: Judgment on a corrupt earth leads to complete destruction.
Theological parallel: The earth's reaction to human sin and ungodliness.
Prophetic parallel: God's wrath that wipes out sinners from the earth.
Theological explanation: The corruption of the earth is due to breaking God's laws/covenant.
Thematic parallel: The earth's grief and corruption under human sin.
Theological interpretation: The flood as a 're-creation' back into chaos (formless and void).
Direct allusion: Confirmation that the flood destroyed the corrupt world.
Theological parallel: God's wrath destroys the ungodly.
Theological parallel: Judgment returns the earth to a state of 'formless and void'.
Theological parallel: The nature of evil (the conception of disaster) leads to judgment.
Theological explanation: God's wrath is revealed against human unrighteousness.
Theological explanation: The source of evil is the human heart.
Theological parallel: The nature of sin leads to death (as in the flood).
